wave_subagent: W5.d (stage-1 SIMD integration: scan_structural wired into parse())
scope_note: AW-III.W5.d closes the stage-1 SIMD pre-pass integration opened by W5.a/b/c. Pre-W5.d the emitted parse() constructed `let idx = StructuralIndex::new()` inline and threaded the empty index through the walker — the bbnf-simd-scan kernel was compiled, benchmarked (4775 MB/s standalone on twitter), and verified correct, but the hot path never invoked it. W5.d wires the pipeline: the emitted parse() body now constructs `STRUCTURAL_ALPHABET: StructuralAlphabet = StructuralAlphabet::from_profile(&GRAMMAR_PROFILE)` as a `const`, calls `bbnf_simd_scan::scan_structural(input.as_bytes(), &STRUCTURAL_ALPHABET)` once per parse, and passes `&idx` through the walker. Walker signature gains `idx: &StructuralIndex` and the inner `__dta_walker_inline::run` accepts it from the caller. The type bridge between `GrammarProfile` and `bbnf_simd_scan::StructuralAlphabet` migrates `structural_digraphs` from `&'static [[u8; 2]]` to `&'static [(u8, u8)]` so the same `.rodata` literal feeds both sides — no shim, no wrapper. samply on twitter post-W5.d confirms `bbnf_simd_scan::neon::scan` at 12.13% self-time (hard-gate proof the kernel runs). The JSON twitter throughput target (≥ 1500 MB/s) is NOT met: twitter measures 170 MB/s, a -11% regression vs W4.d's 192 MB/s. The regression is the SIMD scan's per-parse cost (12% new overhead) that the walker's dual-cursor doesn't yet amortise — the W5.c arm collapse for Regex turned out to be unsound for dense-alphabet grammars (CSS L4 mines `[0..127]` as the structural set; every byte is structural so the bound `[pos, idx.positions[slot])` collapses to zero-width scans) and has been reverted to scan the full input. The Regex bound speedup requires per-pattern alphabet narrowing — IR data the current pass doesn't surface; deferred to the next tranche. Walker consumption of the populated index via slot-advancing remains in place for ByteDispatch (which reads `idx.kinds[slot]` via the W5.c arm) and WsTrim's slot resync — those paths benefit in the absence of the dense-alphabet pathology.

json_twitter_1500_mbps.rationale: W4.d twitter was 192 MB/s; W5.d drops to 170 MB/s (-11%). The drop is the SIMD scan's 12.13% self-time overhead without compensating walker speedup — the W5.c Regex bound collapse turned out to be unsound for dense-alphabet grammars (CSS L4 mines [0..127] as structural; every byte is structural so the bound `[pos, idx.positions[slot])` collapses to zero-width scans and every parse fails at offset 0). The Regex arm reverts to full-input scan in W5.d. Restoring the Regex bound speedup needs per-pattern alphabet narrowing — the IR must surface each regex pattern's matchable byte set so the bound check can verify disjointness from the structural set; deferred to the next tranche. The walker still benefits from ByteDispatch's `idx.kinds[slot]` lookup (one indexed u8 load vs `input.get(pos)` bounds check) and WsTrim's slot-resync path, but those gains don't cover the SIMD scan's overhead at twitter's input size.

type_bridge_summary.before: bbnf_tape::GrammarProfile::structural_digraphs: &'static [[u8; 2]]; bbnf_simd_scan::StructuralAlphabet::digraph_pairs: &'static [(u8, u8)] — distinct shapes required a wrapper layer.
type_bridge_summary.after: Both unify at &'static [(u8, u8)]. The profile emitter lowers `static __GRAMMAR_PROFILE_DIGRAPHS: [(u8, u8); N]`; both the tape-side profile field and the SIMD scanner alphabet's digraph_pairs bind to the same underlying static. `StructuralAlphabet::from_profile(&GrammarProfile) -> Self` is `const fn`, so the parse() entry's `const STRUCTURAL_ALPHABET: StructuralAlphabet = from_profile(&GRAMMAR_PROFILE)` compiles to a .rodata constant with zero construction cost.

samply_attribution_post_w5d.interpretation: The stage-1 SIMD kernel takes 12.13% of walker-parse time on JSON twitter — the pre-pass runs once and produces the StructuralIndex the walker's ByteDispatch arm consults. The W5.c dual-cursor arm rewrites consume the index via `idx.kinds[slot]` (ByteDispatch) and `idx.positions[slot]` (WsTrim slot resync). The remaining walker self-time (36.64%) and scanner self-time (31.92%) dominate because the Regex bound speedup that W5.c claimed was unsound for dense-alphabet grammars and reverts to full-input scan in W5.d. The 170 MB/s twitter throughput vs W4.d's 192 MB/s is a -11% regression — the SIMD pre-pass runs but doesn't amortise on the walker side yet. The next step is per-pattern alphabet narrowing on the IR so the Regex bound can be restored with a disjointness witness, or alternatively lifting `DtaState::ConsumeToNextStructural` out of substrate-only status (the arm landed in W5.c but no lifter emits it today).

regression_rationales.json_twitter_regression: W4.d 192 MB/s → W5.d 170 MB/s (-11%). The SIMD scan runs (12.13% samply self-time) but the walker's Regex bound revert (no longer uses idx.positions[slot] as upper bound) means the regex scanner still walks the full input. Restoring the speedup needs per-pattern alphabet narrowing at the IR.
regression_rationales.css_regression: CSS L4 mines [0..127] as its structural alphabet — every byte is structural, so the SIMD index has ~one entry per input byte. The WsTrim slot-jump and Regex bound both need the alphabet-disjoint precondition which CSS L4 does not satisfy; the arms revert to scalar byte-class path. CSS benches drop 2-3 MB/s due to the SIMD scan overhead without compensating walker speedup.
regression_rationales.path_forward: Two levers remain for W6: (1) IR pass that mines each regex pattern's matchable byte set and emits it as a const alongside GRAMMAR_PROFILE; the Regex arm checks disjointness with the structural set at comptime and re-enables the bound when disjoint. (2) Lift `DtaState::ConsumeToNextStructural` out of substrate status — the arm is wired in the driver but no lifter emits it today. When the lifter identifies a 'scan until delimiter' pattern (JSON number's `[0-9.eE+-]+` terminated by `,]}`), it emits ConsumeToNextStructural instead of the bare Regex; the walker's O(1) cursor jump amortises the SIMD scan's overhead.

honesty_note: The W5.d hard gate of JSON twitter ≥ 1500 MB/s is NOT met (170 MB/s, gap 8.8×). The integration landing is complete and verifiable: (1) parse() constructs the alphabet from GRAMMAR_PROFILE as a const, (2) bbnf_simd_scan::scan_structural runs once per parse and builds the StructuralIndex, (3) the walker accepts the populated index via the dual-cursor interface, (4) samply confirms the kernel runs (12.13% self-time, bbnf_simd_scan::neon::scan hot symbol). The throughput regression is not a W5.d wiring bug — it is the consequence of reverting the W5.c Regex bound collapse that turned out to be unsound for dense-alphabet grammars. Restoring the speedup requires new IR data (per-pattern regex alphabets) and/or new lifter output (ConsumeToNextStructural), both beyond W5.d's integration scope. The path forward is documented above.
